scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: packet forwarding disabled (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward)

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** The Linux `iptables` FORWARD chain on router1.

**Mechanism:** In Linux, the netfilter FORWARD chain intercepts every IPv4 packet that arrives on one interface and needs to be forwarded out another. Unlike INPUT (traffic destined for the router itself) and OUTPUT (traffic originated by the router), the FORWARD chain governs all transit flows. On router1, a single appended rule `-A FORWARD -j DROP` unconditionally drops every transit packet before it can be forwarded, regardless of any routing table entry or FRR configuration. This is confirmed by `iptables-save` output showing `-A FORWARD -j DROP` as the only rule, and by the non-zero packet/byte counter (2 packets / 168 bytes already dropped at inspection time).

**Why local symptoms still work:** The FORWARD DROP does not affect FRR's RIP daemon — RIP hellos are directed at the router's own UDP stack and hit the INPUT chain, not FORWARD, so routes propagate correctly to all routers. Similarly, office_pc's ping to its gateway 192.168.3.1 terminates at router1's own interface (INPUT), which has an ACCEPT policy and no blocking rules.

**Localization:** router1 only. Its FRR routing table, interface addresses, and IP forwarding sysctl (`/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward = 1`) are all correct. The fault lives entirely in the iptables data plane.

**Root cause:** A blanket `-A FORWARD -j DROP` iptables rule was injected on router1, silently blackholing all transit IPv4 traffic through the device.

**Corrective fix:** Remove the rogue rule with `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP`, then delete the corresponding line from `/etc/iptables/rules.v4` (the persisted ruleset shown by `iptables-save`) so it does not survive a restart.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly localizes the issue to router1 (mentions router1 in affected component and localization sections).

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies router1's iptables FORWARD chain drop rule as disabling packet forwarding and notes ip_forward is set, matching the required component.
The diagnosis explicitly states the FORWARD chain drops transit packets while INPUT handles traffic destined to router1 (RIP, pings to 192.168.3.1), clearly distinguishing transit vs local traffic.
Explicitly removes the FORWARD DROP with iptables -D and deletes the persisted rule so forwarding is re-enabled and the change survives reboot.
